OMIM:612164.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 4 is strongly linked to STXBP1. Research papers show STXBP1 changes that make the protein work less. There are also patient studies and group resources you may want to review.

steps.text: Research papers show STXBP1 can cause this condition. The link is well supported.
Several papers say STXBP1 changes may make the protein work less. They describe loss of function, haploinsufficiency, or mRNA breakdown.
Records show STXBP1-related studies and data projects are already underway. These include STARR, ESCO, RARE-X STXBP1, and Simons Searchlight.
Research papers also suggest this condition may look similar to some other epilepsy conditions. That is only a hint, not proof of the same cause.

uncertainties: The records do not show which STXBP1 changes fit each person’s symptoms.
The study notes say some registry entries need confirmation for exact scope.
The similarity links are hypotheses, so they do not prove shared biology.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the STXBP1 claims and the listed studies, especially STARR and ESCO, for fit to your family.

OMIM:613721.summary_plain: Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 11 is strongly linked to SCN2A. Research papers show SCN2A changes can make the sodium channel work too much, too little, or in a mixed way. Several studies and patient resources also include this condition.

steps.text: Research papers show SCN2A causes this condition. That link is well supported. [E00026]
One paper says some SCN2A changes may make the sodium channel work too much. This fits a gain-of-function change. [Mfce5014c]
Another paper says one SCN2A change may make the channel work less, while also showing mixed behavior in cells. That means some changes may not act the same way. [Md58c8bdc, M30b5f5fe]
Records show this condition is being studied in several SCN2A-focused studies, including Elsunersen and PRAX-562. [T00052, T00053, T00054, C00031, C00032, C00033]
Records also show this condition appears in broader patient studies, including Simons Searchlight. [T00058, Y00002, Y00003]

uncertainties: Some SCN2A changes may work differently from others. The mixed and loss-of-function findings come from lab studies, not all patients. [M30b5f5fe, Md58c8bdc]
The study records say SCN2A is in the title or keywords, but they also say the disease fit should be checked. That means the exact group enrolled is not fully clear. [T00052, T00053, T00054, T00058]
So we cannot say which approach helps most. [T00052, T00053, T00054, C00031, C00032, C00033]
The patient-group resources listed are for related conditions and may not be a direct resource for this condition. [C00005, C00007]
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes or a study contact to review the SCN2A change against the three SCN2A study records and the lab findings. This can help judge whether the change looks more like gain, loss, or mixed effect. [Mfce5014c, M30b5f5fe, Md58c8bdc, T00052, T00053, T00054]

OMIM:614558.summary_plain: Research papers and study records show that SCN8A is linked to Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 13. The strongest clue is that SCN8A changes that make the sodium channel work too much are reported in this condition. Several study records also include this condition, which suggests active research and possible patient matching.

steps.text: SCN8A is tied to Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 13 in trusted disease records. This is a supported link, not just a guess. [E00038]

Studies report SCN8A changes that make the sodium channel work too much. One paper says patient-derived SCN8A changes were gain-of-function. Another says gain-of-function changes cause this SCN8A-related encephalopathy. A specific change, R1872W, was reported to impair channel inactivation and cause nerve-cell overactivity and seizures. [M3ed936f1, M8ac04bfa, M71caee27]

There are study records that include this condition, including the EMBOLD trial and two SCN8A-DEE studies. This shows the condition is being followed in research settings. [C00040, T00059, T00060, T00062, T00063]

We also found a study record for a registry and natural history project on epilepsy-dyskinesia syndromes. That suggests researchers are collecting real-world information, but it does not prove one shared cause for every person. [T00062, T00063]

uncertainties: The records do not say which exact SCN8A change applies to your family member.
Some study titles mention SCN8A, but the notes say the disease fit should be confirmed.
The possible shared mechanism with other early infantile encephalopathies is only a hypothesis in the records.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the specific SCN8A change against the supported gain-of-function claims and the study records for EMBOLD and the SCN8A-DEE studies. [M3ed936f1, M8ac04bfa, M71caee27, C00040, T00059, T00060]

OMIM:613720.summary_plain: Research records show that KCNQ2 causes Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 7. Some KCNQ2 changes may make the channel work less, while others may make it work more. Records also show several studies and patient resources for this condition, but some links are only suggestive and need expert review.

steps.text: Research records show KCNQ2 causes Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 7.
Some KCNQ2 changes may make the potassium channel work less.
Other KCNQ2 changes may make the potassium channel work more.
Records show this condition is being studied in several KCNQ2 research projects.
Records also show a KCNQ2 patient registry and a natural history study.

uncertainties: Some study records only say KCNQ2 in the title or keywords, so scope should be checked.
The gain-of-function and loss-of-function findings are tied to different reports, so they do not prove one shared mechanism.
The similarity links to other diseases are only hypotheses, not proof of the same cause.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the KCNQ2 reports and study records, especially E00066, M0b72332f, M0d3df851, and the study records T00031, T00032, and T00033.

OMIM:614959.summary_plain: KCNT1 changes cause Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 14. Research papers also suggest many disease changes make the KCNT1 potassium channel work more, not less. There are study records and a patient registry for this condition.

steps.text: Research papers show KCNT1 causes Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 14. That is the main known cause we found. [E00076]

Several human reports say KCNT1 changes may make the potassium channel work more. The quoted papers describe gain-of-function changes in children with this condition. [M42759263, Mda84cf38, M6bf4475a]
We also found a KCNT1 patient registry and KCNT1-related studies. These include a natural history study and two treatment studies. [C00050, C00051, C00052, T00036, T00037, T00039]
Some records mention other gene conditions that look similar. That similarity is only a hint, not proof of the same cause. [E00239, E00233, E00244]

uncertainties: The study records say KCNT1 in the title or keywords, but each one still needs scope checking. [T00036, T00037, T00039]
We did not find details here about which KCNT1 changes are most common, or how symptoms differ by change. [M42759263, Mda84cf38, M6bf4475a]
The similar-disease links are hypothesis-only and do not show shared biology. [E00239, E00233, E00244]

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the KCNT1 registry and study records, especially the natural history study and the two KCNT1 treatment studies. [C00050, C00051, C00052, T00036, T00037, T00039]

OMIM:612621.summary_plain: Research papers show that changes in SYNGAP1 cause Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 5. The strongest pattern is loss of function, which means the gene makes its protein work less. Records also show this condition is being studied in natural history and autism-related studies.

steps.text: Research papers show that SYNGAP1 causes this condition.
Several papers say SYNGAP1 changes may make the protein work less. That loss-of-function pattern is supported in people with this condition.
Records show this condition is included in studies that follow patients over time. These include Simons Searchlight, STARR, and FENDEEP.
Research papers also show overlap with seizure and development problems seen in other rare brain conditions. That overlap is only a clue, not proof of a shared cause.

uncertainties: The study notes say some records need confirmation of exact scope for SYNGAP1 or the related condition.
The overlap with other conditions is a hypothesis, not proven shared biology.
This list does not show whether age, exact change type, or symptoms affect study fit.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask the study team or a doctor who knows genes to review the cited SYNGAP1 natural history records and confirm which ones accept your family’s exact change.

OMIM:300672.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 2 is strongly linked to changes in CDKL5. Records show those changes usually make CDKL5 work less, which fits this condition. We also found patient study resources and natural history studies that may help families and experts learn more.

steps.text: Records show CDKL5 causes Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 2. This is the main known link for this condition. [E00128]

Research papers show CDKL5 changes may make the protein work less. One paper says the change can lower CDKL5 catalytic activity. Another says CDKL5 mutations cause enzymatic loss of function. [Mf6524880, Meaf2ee41, M01118803]

We also found family and study resources for CDKL5. These include the International CDKL5 Registry, the International CDKL5 Disorder Database, and the International CDKL5 Clinical Research Network. [C00065, C00066, C00067]

Records show this condition is being studied in a registry-style study and a clinical research network study. These records may help families find more natural history information. [T00020, T00021, T00024, T00001]

uncertainties: The study records do not prove the exact patient group included. Several notes say the disease or change should be confirmed. [T00020, T00021, T00024, T00001]
The listed study records are about study enrollment or readiness, not outcomes. [T00020, T00021, T00024, T00001]
The similarity links to other conditions are only hypotheses. They are not proof of the same disease process. [E00246, E00225, E00250]
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the CDKL5 loss-of-function claims and the CDKL5 study records together. Ask whether the registry or research network fit your family’s situation. [Mf6524880, Meaf2ee41, M01118803, T00020, T00021, T00024, C00065, C00066, C00067]

OMIM:615473.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 17 is tied to GNAO1. Research papers also suggest this condition may involve changes that make G protein signaling work too much or in a dominant-negative way, but those animal findings need expert review.

steps.text: Research papers show GNAO1 causes Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 17. That is the main known link for this condition.

We found animal studies where GNAO1 changes may make G protein signaling work too much. These studies support a possible gain-of-function pattern, but they do not prove every patient has the same change.
We also found an animal study that suggests a dominant-negative change for GNAO1. That means the changed gene may interfere with the normal one, but this is still a research finding.

There are study records for this condition, including a GNAO1 natural history study and several GNAO1-focused research projects. These records show active research support, not a proven treatment path.
Records also show a few GNAO1 support and study resources. These can help families connect with research teams and learn what is being studied.

uncertainties: The animal findings do not tell us which change, if any, applies to a specific person.
The records do not give clear patient results, so we cannot say which research study helps which child.
The similarity links to other seizure conditions are only hypotheses, not proof of shared cause.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the GNAO1 papers and the listed GNAO1 study records together, so you can check whether any family member matches the research scope.

OMIM:607745.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3 is linked to SCN2A. Research also suggests some SCN2A changes make the sodium channel work less. There are support groups and research studies connected to SCN2A, but they may not all fit this exact condition.

steps.text: Research papers show SCN2A causes Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3. This is a well-supported link for this condition. [E00175]
One study reports an SCN2A change that made the sodium channel work less in the lab. That result supports a possible loss-of-function change, but it is still a lab finding. [M13d4d49b]
Records also show a similar condition, Seizures, benign familial infantile, 5, may share symptoms. That is only a suggestion, not proof of the same cause. [E00252]
We also found a family group for SCN2A-related disease, including this condition. That may help with patient support and study updates. [C00004]

uncertainties: The lab finding is only from one quoted study, so it may not apply to every SCN2A change. [M13d4d49b]
The similar-condition link is a hypothesis, not proof of shared biology. [E00252]
The research study records linked to SCN2A mostly name broader SCN2A-DEE or other conditions, so it is unclear which ones fit this exact condition. [C00031, C00032]
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN2A finding and the support group link together. They can help decide whether the lab result and family group are useful for your family. [E00175, M13d4d49b, C00004]

OMIM:617080.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial infantile, 5 is linked to SCN8A. Research papers also suggest a change in SCN8A may make a sodium channel work more. There are patient groups and related studies for SCN8A, but not a study named for this exact condition.

steps.text: Research papers show SCN8A causes this condition. That link is well supported.
One report suggests some SCN8A changes may make the sodium channel work more. This is based on one described case, so it is suggestive, not final.
There is a hypothesis that this condition may be similar to Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3. That shared pattern is not proof of the same cause.
We also found patient groups that serve people with this condition. These groups may be useful for support and updates.
Records show SCN8A has related studies of seizure care in SCN8A-DEE. These studies are related, but they are not shown here as studies for this exact condition.

uncertainties: We do not see a study listed here for Seizures, benign familial infantile, 5 by name.
The variant effect evidence is from one quoted report, so it may not apply to every SCN8A change.
The similarity to Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3 is only a hypothesis and needs expert review.
We do not have details here about which SCN8A changes are most common in this condition.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN8A cause link and the one gain-of-function report together, using OMIM:617080 and PMID:34431999.

OMIM:121200.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial neonatal, 1 is strongly linked to KCNQ2. Research papers also suggest some KCNQ2 changes make the protein work less. Some records show KCNQ2-focused studies and a patient group resource, but not specific care advice for this condition.

steps.text: Research papers show KCNQ2 causes Seizures, benign familial neonatal, 1. This is a strong, curated link. [E00187]
Research papers also show some KCNQ2 changes make the protein work less. That fits a loss-of-function pattern in this condition. [M469654af, M05787647]

One study report says two KCNQ2 changes at the same spot had opposite effects in lab tests. One change increased protein pieces, while the other decreased them. That suggests change-specific effects, but it is still lab evidence. [Md1dba723]
Records also show a KCNQ2 patient group resource for this condition. That can help families find disease-focused information. [C00010]

Other records show KCNQ2-focused studies, including XEN496 (Ezogabine) and an omics study. These records show research interest, but they do not prove benefit for this condition. [T00031, T00032, C00042, C00043, C00044]

uncertainties: The study records do not confirm results for people with this condition. They only show that the studies exist. [T00031, T00032, C00042, C00043, C00044]
The lab findings describe specific KCNQ2 changes, not all changes. We cannot assume every change acts the same way. [Md1dba723, M469654af, M05787647]
We do not have direct care guidance, symptom timing details, or family history data here. [E00187, Md1dba723, M469654af, M05787647]

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the KCNQ2 change in your family and compare it with the lab findings and KCNQ2 study records. [E00187, Md1dba723, M469654af, M05787647, T00031, T00032, C00042, C00043, C00044]

OMIM:607208.summary_plain: Research papers show that SCN1A changes are a known cause of Dravet syndrome. The strongest records say these changes usually make the sodium channel work less. We also found several studies and patient-list efforts, but some are for related conditions, not this one.

steps.text: Research papers show SCN1A causes Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 6 (Dravet syndrome).
More papers say SCN1A changes usually make the sodium channel work less.
We also found Dravet syndrome studies and follow-up records, which may help families track research.

uncertainties: Some study records only say SCN1A is in the title or keywords. They still need expert checking for exact fit.
The related-condition studies for SCN8A and SCN2A are not direct evidence for this condition.
The similarity links to other conditions are only guesses.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN1A cause claim and the listed Dravet study records together.
